newsitem.title: UK: Investor analysts say Mexico rebels only irritation.
newsitem.headline: Investor analysts say Mexico rebels only irritation.

text.p: Mexico's worst political violence in two years is little more than a nuisance and will not deflect investors' attention from an increasingly attractive economy, investment analysts said on Friday.
"Investors won't stay away from a good economic story," Latinvest Securities analyst Sarah Lavers said.
She said the stock market and the peso had been so strong recently that surprise rebel attacks this week in Mexico were mostly a good excuse for investors to cash in some of their profits.
Mexican stocks, bonds and the peso have all fallen in the past two days.
Since Wednesday, hundreds of heavily-armed guerrillas from a little known revolutionary group have stormed villages in central and southern Mexico.
At least 12 people have died in what is the worst political violence in the country since the Zapatista rebellion erupted in the southeastern state of Chiapas.
On Friday, the Mexican army was braced for fresh attacks by the self-styled Popular Revolutionary Army which is demanding the overthrow of the government of President Ernesto Zedillo.
The rebellion has come as the country is emerging, glittering, from more than a year of severe recession which followed the collapse of the peso and near economic ruin in late 1994.
"It's just noise. The political situation is stable...and the economic programme is working," ANZ economist Jerome Booth said.
He expected the solid progress of the economy to be highlighted by Zedillo in his state of the union address on Sunday.

"My argument is that it (the rebellion) represents a buying opportunity. It is not likely to extend into generalised insurrection or require a big hand-out of money," Bank of America analyst Richard Gray said.
Latinvest's Lavers said the attacks were the first warning shot in the run-up to next year's Congressional elections, showing that Zedillo would not find it easy to impose his reforms.
She pointed to the strong opposition from the so-called "dinosaurs" of the ruling Institional Revolutionary Party (PRI) which has ruled Mexico for much of this century.
However, she predicted Zedillo would win and the old-guard of the PRI would lose power.
"(The rebellion) is more a thorn is the side of the government than a systemic crisis," West Merchant Bank economic adviser Peter West said.

"It is a useful reminder that social problems and poverty are acute and that broad sectors of the economy have not been touched by the recovery...But it doesn't change the underlying (positive) story," he added.
